chapter_title: Advanced Application Security Testing and Remediation

screens.title: Advanced Application Security Testing and Remediation
screens.subtitle: Layered testing strategies, runtime protection, and effective remediation workflows

narration.text: In this chapter you'll learn how to test applications at every stage of their lifecycle and then remediate what you find. We'll distinguish four automated approaches — static, dynamic, interactive testing, and runtime self-protection — and place each where it gives the most value. You will also see how human testing, like penetration testing and bug bounty programs, complements automated tools. Practical remediation follows detection: we will cover prioritization, root-cause analysis, and how to feed fixes back into your secure software development lifecycle. For example, a static scanner can flag unsafe string concatenation in code so developers fix it before merge, while a dynamic scanner can find a login page that leaks user enumeration at runtime. This layered approach reduces false positives, narrows investigation time, and improves overall security posture. As you move through the chapter, think about which tools you would run in a pre-commit hook, which belong in a CI pipeline, and which need a running staging environment. That mental model will help you design an effective testing program and prioritize remediation work that reduces real business risk.

keyIdea.title: Layer testing across code and runtime
keyIdea.text: Combine early static analysis with runtime and interactive testing, then remediate by prioritizing risk and fixing root causes.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to name and differentiate SAST, DAST, IAST, and RASP, design a layered testing strategy that uses the right tool at the right time, and analyze test results to prioritize remediation. You will also understand when to engage manual testing like penetration tests or a bug bounty program and how to manage those engagements responsibly. For example, you will be able to explain why a SAST tool belongs in a pre-commit or CI step to catch string concatenation vulnerabilities, and why DAST requires a running staging environment to detect authentication or configuration issues. You will practice taking a scan output, determining exploitability and business impact, and producing a remediation plan that includes re-testing and developer guidance. Finally, you'll be able to recommend runtime protections when code fixes are not immediately possible. These objectives are practical: they help you reduce time-to-fix, cut down on false positives, and build safer deployment pipelines.

narration.text: These additional objectives focus on remediation, verification, and continuous improvement. You will learn to craft remediation plans that go beyond a quick patch to address root causes, apply re-testing to confirm fixes, and incorporate lessons into secure coding standards. For example, after fixing a S Q L injection instance, you will run a full SAST sweep and targeted DAST checks, then update secure coding guidelines to mandate parameterized queries. You will also learn how to balance quick production mitigations — such as RASP or temporary input validation — with longer-term code fixes, and how to avoid common mistakes like fixing symptoms without addressing systemic causes. Finally, you will practice communicating prioritized findings to developers and product owners so that fixes align with business needs. These skills reduce recurrence, lower remediation cost, and foster a culture that learns from vulnerabilities.

screens.title: Static Application Security Testing (SAST)
screens.subtitle: Source-code analysis and early feedback for developers

narration.text: Static Application Security Testing examines source, bytecode, or binaries without running the application. It looks for known insecure patterns — for example, building S Q L queries with string concatenation — and surfaces them as code-level findings. SAST is a shift-left technique: run it in the IDE, as a pre-commit hook, or in CI to give developers fast feedback and reduce later remediation cost. A concrete example in the chapter shows an insecure Java method that concatenates user input into an S Q L string and a secure replacement using a prepared statement with a parameterized query. The secure change prevents S Q L injection by separating data from executable query text. While SAST is powerful for early detection, it often reports false positives or flags issues that may not be exploitable in the running context. It also cannot see runtime configuration flaws, authentication bypasses, or how deployed services interact. A common misconception is that SAST alone makes an application secure. In practice, treat SAST as a preventative layer; pair it with runtime tests and re-testing after fixes. Takeaway: use SAST early to catch code smells and prevent many bugs before they reach staging.

keyIdea.title: SAST is early detection
keyIdea.text: Analyze code without execution to find patterns like SQL injection, but expect false positives and complement with runtime tests.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.8 › SAST
Definition

Static Application Security Testing

Analyze code artifacts without execution to find vulnerability patterns before deployment.

Why use SAST?
  • Finds code-level issues early when fixes are cheaper.
  • Integrates with IDEs to give immediate developer feedback.
  • Helps enforce secure coding patterns across repos.
Common Pitfall
High false positive rates; tool tuning and ruleset review reduce noise.
Pro tip
Integrate SAST into pre-commit and CI jobs with progressive enforcement to avoid developer friction.
Key Takeaway

SAST prevents many vulnerabilities cheaply but must be paired with runtime testing and tuned to reduce false positives.

Code Example
<!-- Insecure Java code flagged by SAST -->
public List<User> searchUsers(String query) {
  String sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '" + query + "'"; // Vulnerable to SQL Injection
  // ... execute query ...
}

// Secure Java code using PreparedStatement
public List<User> searchUsersSecure(String query) {
  String sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = ?";
  PreparedStatement ps = connection.prepareStatement(sql);
  ps.setString(1, query); // Parameterized query prevents SQL injection
  // ... execute query ...
}
Example explanation
The insecure example builds SQL by concatenating user input. A SAST tool flags that pattern. The secure replacement uses parameterized queries to separate data and code.

screens.title: SAST Limitations and Best Practices
screens.subtitle: Tuning, false positives, and integration patterns

narration.text: SAST is essential, but understanding its limits makes it effective in practice. SAST often produces false positives because it reasons about code paths without runtime context. For instance, a flagged S Q L concatenation might only be reachable in a test harness or require authentication steps that don't exist in reported traces. To make SAST usable, tune rules, prioritize findings by likely exploitability, and combine SAST results with IAST or manual review for confirmation. Integrate SAST into developer workflows: IDE plugins for instant feedback, pre-commit scans for quick checks, and CI jobs for enforced gates. A progressive enforcement strategy reduces developer pushback — surface warnings early and enforce only high-confidence rules as blocking checks. Use SAST findings as training material for secure coding sessions and incorporate custom rules that reflect your application's frameworks and patterns. Misconception to avoid: turning off noisy checks entirely. Instead, triage and tune rulesets, and ensure findings feed a remediation backlog. The practical outcome is reduced noise, faster remediation, and clearer developer guidance on how to fix root causes rather than symptoms. SAST Limitations and Best Practices means reduce noise with rule tuning, progressive enforcement, and combining sast with contextual testing to confirm exploitability.. In practical terms, tuning, false positives, and integration patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Tune SAST for action
keyIdea.text: Reduce noise with rule tuning, progressive enforcement, and combining SAST with contextual testing to confirm exploitability.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.8 › SAST Best Practices

Limitations & Risk

Understand false positives, missing runtime context, and rule set maintenance.

False positives
Expect tool noise; triage with sample inputs and runtime confirmation.
Progressive enforcement
Warn early, block only high-confidence rules, and increase coverage over time.
Rule customization
Adjust rules for your frameworks and common patterns to reduce irrelevant alerts.
Integration patterns
IDE plugin
Immediate developer feedback as code is written.
Pre-commit checks
Fast local scan to catch obvious issues before push.
CI gate
Run full SAST as part of CI with reporting and tracked findings.
Misconception: disabling noisy rules removes risk. Better to tune and triage than to ignore tool output.

screens.title: Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST)
screens.subtitle: Testing a running application by simulating attacks

narration.text: Dynamic Application Security Testing targets a running application. It simulates attacker behaviors against exposed interfaces like web pages and APIs to find runtime flaws: authentication issues, session problems, misconfigurations, and input handling errors. DAST tools act like automated penetration testers. The chapter highlights common DAST tools and a hands-on activity that walks through OWASP ZAP: set up a vulnerable app, run an automated scan, then review alerts such as S Q L injection or cross-site scripting. A concrete scenario: a DAST scan of a staging login page might reveal username enumeration via differing response messages. Because DAST interacts only with external surfaces, it is language-agnostic and discovers issues SAST cannot, yet it usually cannot point to the exact line of code. DAST requires a running environment and careful scope — never scan production without permission. A common misconception is that DAST will find every runtime flaw; it cannot cover internal logic paths that require specific authenticated flows unless those flows are explored during testing. Takeaway: use DAST in staging and pre-production as a reality check against runtime exposures, and pair findings with SAST or IAST to locate the underlying code.

keyIdea.title: DAST finds runtime issues
keyIdea.text: Run automated attacks against a live app to detect authentication, session, and configuration vulnerabilities, then confirm with code context.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.8 › DAST
Definition

Dynamic Application Security Testing

Simulate attacks against a running app to find issues that only appear in execution context.

Typical findings
  • Authentication and session flaws
  • Input validation gaps like XSS or SQL injection visible at runtime
  • Misconfigurations exposing sensitive data
Safety note
Only scan systems you own or are authorized to test. Avoid production without explicit planning.
Process Example

Set up staging, run the automated DAST scan, inspect alerts, then verify exploitable findings manually.

Hands-on: OWASP ZAP
Quick steps
  1. Deploy a vulnerable app like Juice Shop on localhost.
  2. Launch OWASP ZAP and enter the app URL.
  3. Run an automated scan and review the Alerts tab for high severity issues.
DAST advantage: language-agnostic testing of exposed interfaces. Limitation: limited code visibility.

screens.title: Interactive Application Security Testing (IAST)
screens.subtitle: Combining static and dynamic insights with runtime instrumentation

narration.text: Interactive Application Security Testing instruments the application while it runs, capturing data flow, execution paths, and HTTP traffic to present high-confidence findings with actionable code locations. IAST agents inside the runtime give you the best of both worlds: the precision of SAST with the context of DAST. For example, an IAST agent can show the exact method and line where unvalidated input reaches a database call during a specific request, dramatically reducing investigation time. IAST reduces false positives because it observes real executions; however, it requires deploying instrumentation in environments where tests exercise application behavior. A key practical use is to run IAST during integration tests in CI or during an automated test run in staging. Misconception: IAST replaces manual testing. It doesn't — human testers still find complex business logic flaws and chained exploits. Instead, treat IAST as a powerful tool for accurate, contextual diagnostics that speeds developer fixes and improves the signal-to-noise ratio of automated testing. Interactive Application Security Testing (IAST) means instrument the running app to get accurate, code-located findings that combine sast accuracy with dast context.. In practical terms, combining static and dynamic insights with runtime instrumentation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: IAST = context + precision
keyIdea.text: Instrument the running app to get accurate, code-located findings that combine SAST accuracy with DAST context.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.8 › IAST
Definition

Interactive Application Security Testing

IAST instruments the runtime to monitor execution, data flow, and request context for precise findings.

How IAST helps
  • Links runtime evidence to specific code locations.
  • Reduces false positives by observing real executions.
  • Gives precise remediation steps to developers.
Deployment model
Run IAST as an agent during integration tests or test jobs where real application paths are exercised.
Example
Observed flow
IAST reports that request X passed user input through method Y into database call Z, and highlights the vulnerable line for quick fixes.
Misconception
IAST is not a replacement for human testing; it complements manual efforts by clarifying exploitability and root cause.

screens.title: Runtime Application Self-Protection (RASP)
screens.subtitle: Inline runtime protection that understands application context

narration.text: Runtime Application Self-Protection runs inside the application or its runtime to detect and block attacks in real time. Unlike a Web Application Firewall that sits at the edge, RASP has direct visibility into application logic and data flow, so it can make informed decisions about whether a request is malicious. For example, if a RASP agent sees an attempted S Q L injection it can block the query from reaching the database, even if the code is vulnerable. RASP is useful when immediate protection is required while a permanent code fix is scheduled. However, RASP requires careful tuning because aggressive blocking could disrupt legitimate users or add latency. A common misconception is that RASP substitutes for secure coding; it’s a defense-in-depth control to reduce risk when perfect remediation is not yet possible. In practice, deploy RASP selectively, monitor false positives closely, and plan to remove it once code-level fixes and process improvements reduce the underlying risk. Runtime Application Self-Protection (RASP) means rasp blocks attacks inside the app using application context, but should be tuned and paired with code fixes to avoid disruptions.. In practical terms, inline runtime protection that understands application context. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: RASP for inline defense
keyIdea.text: RASP blocks attacks inside the app using application context, but should be tuned and paired with code fixes to avoid disruptions.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.8 › RASP
Definition

Runtime Application Self-Protection

Embedded runtime protection that inspects application behavior and blocks malicious actions in real time.

Capabilities
Detects anomalous input, prevents exploitation, and can terminate sessions or requests.
Caution
Requires tuning; false positives or performance impact can disrupt users if misconfigured.
Key Takeaway

RASP provides inline protection when immediate mitigation is needed, but it complements secure code fixes rather than replacing them.

Comparison
WAF
Edge filtering, less visibility into application internals.
RASP
Runtime context, can block inside the app with accurate logic awareness.
Deployment note
Use RASP as a temporary guardrail while prioritizing code fixes and process changes.

screens.title: Penetration Testing and Scope Management
screens.subtitle: Manual testing to uncover business logic and chained vulnerabilities

narration.text: Penetration testing is a manual, goal-oriented exercise where skilled testers emulate an attacker to find and exploit vulnerabilities that automated tools often miss. Pen testers apply reconnaissance, scanning, exploitation, and post-exploitation techniques to show practical impact. A key responsibility for a security practitioner is scoping the engagement: define targets, allowed techniques, timeline, and rules of engagement to avoid unintended disruption. For instance, scope should clearly state whether destructive actions and social engineering are allowed, and how findings are reported. Pen tests are especially valuable for uncovering complex business logic flaws or multi-step exploit chains that tools cannot stitch together. However, pen tests are time-bound snapshots; they should complement continuous automated testing, not replace it. Misconception: a passed pen test means perpetual security. Instead, use pen testing results to prioritize remediation, train developers on identified weaknesses, and update threat models. The deliverable from a pen test should include reproducible steps, impact assessment, and suggested mitigations so teams can remediate and re-test effectively. In practical terms, manual testing to uncover business logic and chained vulnerabilities. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Penetration Testing

A human-led simulated attack focusing on real exploitability and business impact.

Engagement scope
Define targets, permitted techniques, timing, and reporting expectations to prevent disruption.
Deliverables
Repro steps, impact assessment, suggested mitigations, and re-test criteria.
When to use pen testing
  • Before major releases or after significant architecture changes.
  • To validate business logic and complex exploit paths.
Misconception
Passing a pen test is not permanent assurance; it is a snapshot that must be followed by fixes and continuous testing.

screens.title: Bug Bounty Programs
screens.subtitle: Crowdsourced testing with program management considerations

narration.text: Bug bounty programs invite external researchers to find vulnerabilities in exchange for rewards. They extend your testing coverage by crowdsourcing diverse skills and perspectives, often uncovering unusual or creative attack paths. However, managing a bug bounty requires a robust disclosure policy, clear scope, and triage capacity. You must be ready to validate incoming reports quickly and handle sensitive information responsibly. Bug bounties can uncover new classes of bugs that internal teams miss, but they also require careful operational investment: handling duplicates, verifying valid findings, paying bounties, and updating policies. A misconception is relying solely on a bounty program for security. Because bounties are continuous and reactive, they should complement structured SSDLC controls and automated testing. Use bounties to augment bug discovery, and ensure program rules prevent unauthorized testing of production or sensitive subsystems. Finally, feed validated bounty findings back into SAST rules, developer training, and architectural fixes to prevent recurrence. screens.title: Remediation Workflow and Prioritization
screens.subtitle: From finding to fix: triage, root cause, and re-test

narration.text: Effective remediation requires disciplined triage and a focus on root cause rather than quick symptom fixes. Start by assessing severity, exploitability, and business impact — the OWASP Risk Rating approach is helpful for structuring this decision. A prioritized remediation plan includes immediate mitigations for critical paths, scheduled fixes for high-severity issues, and longer-term architecture or process changes for systemic problems. The chapter describes important steps: re-test the specific fix, run broader scans (SAST and DAST) to ensure similar patterns are not present elsewhere, and conduct a root cause analysis to update coding standards or architecture. A concrete example: after fixing an S Q L injection in one endpoint, re-run SAST across the codebase to find other concatenated queries and add a secure-data-access guideline requiring parameterized queries. Common mistakes include treating remediation as a checkbox or failing to re-test. Make remediation visible: create a ticket with reproduction steps, expected fix, test plan, and acceptance criteria. Outcome: durable fixes, fewer regressions, and a feedback loop that reduces repeated vulnerabilities. Remediation Workflow and Prioritization means prioritize by risk, re-test fixes, and update policies and training to prevent recurrence of common vulnerability patterns.. In practical terms, from finding to fix: triage, root cause, and re-test. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 9 › Chapter 9.8 › Remediation

Remediation Workflow

Triage findings, perform root-cause analysis, implement fixes, and re-test to confirm closure.

Triage checklist
  • Severity and exploitability
  • Business impact and affected assets
  • Mitigation options and timelines
Root cause actions
Fix code paths, update secure coding rules, and adjust architecture as needed.
Re-test
Verify the specific fix and run broader scans to ensure no regression elsewhere.
Example action
After a SQL injection fix, re-run SAST across the codebase and update secure access patterns in coding guidelines.
Key mistake: fixing only the symptom. Always ask why the flaw occurred and how to stop it from repeating.

screens.title: Designing a Comprehensive Testing Strategy
screens.subtitle: Integrate automated and manual testing into CI/CD and SSDLC

narration.text: A comprehensive testing strategy places different tests at the stages of the SSDLC where they add the most value. Start with SAST in developer IDEs and pre-commit checks to prevent introducing obvious coding errors. During CI, run IAST during integration tests so you capture execution context and precise code locations. Use DAST against deployed staging environments to simulate external attacker interactions. For production, consider RASP for temporary runtime protection on critical services while permanent fixes are scheduled. Manual testing like pen tests should be scheduled periodically or before major releases, and bug bounty programs provide continuous external coverage. The strategy should be automated where possible and tied to gates and acceptance criteria in your CI/CD pipeline: fail builds for high-confidence critical issues, create tickets for medium-risk findings, and warn on low-risk items while capturing them for trending and training. Misconception: more tools does not equal better security; design the pipeline so each tool addresses a gap, reduces false positives, and minimizes developer interruption. Outcome: a predictable testing cadence that gives developers timely feedback and security teams focused alerts. Designing a Comprehensive Testing Strategy means sast early, iast in integration, dast in staging, rasp in production as needed — coordinate tools with ci/cd gates and policies.. In practical terms, integrate automated and manual testing into ci/cd and ssdlc. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Testing Placement in the Pipeline

Map each testing type to the SSDLC stage where it prevents the most risk.

Developer & Pre-commit

CI / Integration

Staging & Pre-release

Production

Design gates: fail CI for critical issues, create tracked tickets for medium issues, and warn on low issues while collecting metrics for training.

screens.title: Analyzing Security Testing Reports
screens.subtitle: From alerts to actionable remediation tickets

narration.text: Security reports from SAST, DAST, IAST, or pen testing are raw data; your job is to turn them into prioritized action. Start by validating each alert: reproduce it with a test case or request to confirm exploitability. Then categorize by severity and business impact, documenting affected endpoints, reproduction steps, and suggested fixes. Use the findings to create developer-facing remediation tickets with acceptance criteria and re-test steps. For example, a DAST alert showing username enumeration should include a reproduction request, explanation of how it leaks information, and a recommended fix like uniform response messages or rate-limiting. When a SAST report flags multiple concatenated queries, a single ticket requiring parameterized data access patterns and a full-code search to find similar patterns is more effective than dozens of isolated fixes. Misconception: treating every alert as equally urgent. Instead, prioritize by exploitability and asset value so teams focus on the highest business risk first. Finally, ensure every closed ticket is re-tested with the appropriate automated scan and, when relevant, a manual confirmation to prevent regressions. Analyzing Security Testing Reports means validate and reproduce findings, prioritize by risk, and create remediation tickets with acceptance and re-test steps.. In practical terms, from alerts to actionable remediation tickets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Simulating a Basic DAST Scan with OWASP ZAP
screens.subtitle: Practical steps to scan and interpret results safely

narration.text: This hands-on activity walks you through a safe, local DAST scan using OWASP ZAP against a deliberately vulnerable application. First, deploy a vulnerable test app in an isolated environment, such as an intentionally insecure package running on localhost. Next, launch OWASP ZAP, enter the app URL, and run an automated scan. When alerts appear, select a high-severity item like S Q L injection or cross-site scripting. Read the alert description and suggested solution to understand why the tool flagged it. Reproduce the issue manually where safe and confined to the test environment. Then, consult the solution or mitigation notes: implement a fix such as parameterized queries or proper output encoding, and re-run the scan to confirm the alert clears. Important safety guidance: never run DAST against systems you don't own or have explicit permission to test, and avoid scanning production. This exercise shows how DAST finds runtime exposures and how to close the loop from detection to verified remediation in a controlled, ethical setting. Simulating a Basic DAST Scan with OWASP ZAP means run a controlled scan in an isolated environment, review alerts, reproduce safely, implement fixes, and re-test to confirm remediation.. Module 9 › Chapter 9.8 › DAST Lab

Lab: OWASP ZAP Scan

Use a controlled vulnerable app, run an automated scan, and validate alerts safely.

Steps
  1. Deploy a vulnerable web app locally for testing.
  2. Open OWASP ZAP and point it to the app URL.
  3. Run an automated scan and review alerts in the Alerts tab.
  4. Reproduce a high-priority alert safely and apply a fix.
  5. Re-scan to verify remediation.
Safety Note
Only scan systems you control or where you have explicit authorization. Never target production without agreement.
Interpreting alerts
Open the alert details, read the description, solution, and other info to form a remediation plan.
Outcome
Practice the detection-to-remediation cycle: detect, reproduce, fix, re-test, and document.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: We’ve covered four automated testing approaches and two human-driven techniques, plus remediation practices. Remember: SAST analyzes code early to prevent issues, but can produce false positives; DAST tests a running app to find runtime and configuration problems; IAST instruments the runtime to provide precise, code-located findings; and RASP provides inline runtime defense when immediate protection is needed. Penetration testing finds complex, chained, or business-logic vulnerabilities that tools miss, while bug bounty programs extend coverage through crowdsourced research but require operational readiness. For remediation, prioritize by exploitability and business impact, perform root cause analysis, re-test fixes, and update coding guidelines and SSDLC gates so the same issues do not recur. Use a layered strategy: place tools where they give the most leverage — SAST early, IAST in integration, DAST in staging, and RASP selectively in production — and treat manual testing as complementary. The core idea is not to rely on a single tool but to build a measured, repeatable program that reduces risk and enables quicker, more accurate remediation.

keyIdea.text: SAST, IAST, DAST, and RASP work together with pen testing and bounties; remediation should focus on root causes and re-testing.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders to guide your practice

narration.text: Keep three compact reminders front of mind as you apply these techniques. First, choose the right tool for the phase: SAST early in development, IAST in integration tests, DAST against staging, and RASP selectively in production. Second, prioritize remediations by exploitability and business impact; always perform root cause analysis and re-test to confirm fixes. Third, combine automated and human testing—use pen tests and bug bounties to surface logic defects and chained exploits that tools might miss. These three ideas will help you design a testing and remediation program that reduces noise, speeds remediation, and produces lasting improvements to your application security posture. When you encounter an alert, ask: how exploitable is this, what does it affect, and what will prevent it happening again?
